Someone who is snooty believes they are better than other people — better in terms of wealth, social class, taste, or refinement — and they show this belief through cold, dismissive, or superior behavior toward others. It's not just an internal feeling of pride; snooty people make others feel looked down upon.
The Attitude Behind It

A snooty person carries a quiet (sometimes not so quiet) contempt for people they see as being below their level. They treat someone differently depending on how "important," wealthy, educated, or cultured they think that person is. If you don't meet their standard, they simply act as though you're not worth their full attention or respect.

Think of it this way: a snooty person has an invisible scale in their head, and they're constantly measuring whether you're worthy of being treated warmly.
How It Looks in Real Life

Snooty behavior can show up in many ways:

  • Giving someone a cold, barely-there greeting while being warm and friendly to someone else they consider more "important"
  • Speaking in a dismissive or bored tone, as if talking to you is a waste of their time
  • Turning up their nose at your choices — where you shop, what you eat, what music you like, or where you went to school
  • Making comments that subtly (or not so subtly) put you down
  • Refusing to mix with people they consider "ordinary" or beneath them
  • Acting as though certain restaurants, brands, neighborhoods, or events are simply too low-class for them

A snooty waiter, for example, might ignore a casually dressed customer while fussing over someone in an expensive suit. A snooty classmate might roll their eyes when you mention your favorite TV show, as if only people with poor taste would watch it.
Key Examples in Sentences

• "The receptionist at the luxury hotel was so snooty — she looked us up and down before even saying hello."
  • "He can be very snooty about wine. If it's not expensive, he won't drink it."
  • "I didn't feel welcome in that shop. The staff had a snooty attitude the entire time."
  • "She gave a snooty little laugh when I told her I took the bus to work."
  • "Don't be snooty about other people's reading choices — not everyone has to read literary fiction."
  • "The school has a reputation for being snooty — they only seem to care about students from wealthy families."
What Makes Someone Snooty

Snootiness usually comes from one or more of these things:

  • Wealth — having money (or wanting to appear to)
  • Social class — belonging (or trying to belong) to an upper-class background
  • Education — having studied at prestigious schools and looking down on those who haven't
  • Taste — thinking one's preferences in food, art, fashion, or culture are superior
  • Status — holding a high professional or social position

Crucially, a person doesn't have to actually be wealthy or elite to be snooty. Some people who have very little act snooty because they want to be seen as refined or above others. The attitude is what makes someone snooty, not necessarily their real circumstances.
What Snooty Does NOT Mean

Snooty ≠ Shy or Reserved
A shy person is quiet or withdrawn because they feel nervous or unsure. A snooty person is cold or dismissive because they think they're too good for you. The difference is the reason: insecurity vs. a sense of superiority.

Snooty ≠ Simply Rude
A rude person is unpleasant to everyone. A snooty person is selectively unpleasant — they treat people differently based on perceived status. They can be perfectly charming to someone they consider important, while being cold and dismissive to someone they see as beneath them. That selectivity is the hallmark of snootiness.

Snooty ≠ Having High Standards
Having high standards for quality is not snooty in itself. What makes it snooty is when you look down on and dismiss people who don't share or meet those standards. For example, preferring organic food is a personal choice. Sneering at a friend for eating fast food and acting like they're beneath you — that's snooty.
Can Things (Not Just People) Be Snooty?

Yes, though less commonly. When we describe a place or thing as snooty, we mean it has the feel of a snooty person — exclusive, cold, and unwelcoming to anyone who doesn't fit a certain image.

  • "That club has a snooty atmosphere — the bouncers judge you by what you're wearing."
  • "The magazine has a snooty tone, as if it's writing only for the ultra-rich."
How It Feels to Be on the Receiving End

When a snooty person interacts with you, you typically feel:

  • Put down or made to feel "not good enough"
  • Judged for your background, clothes, accent, or tastes
  • Unwelcome, like you don't belong
  • Invisible or unimportant

This is why "snooty" is almost always used as a negative word. Nobody sees being called snooty as a compliment.
Register and Tone of the Word

"Snooty" is an informal word. You'd use it in everyday conversation and casual writing. It carries a slightly playful or critical edge — when someone calls a person snooty, they're gently (or not so gently) criticizing that behavior.

In formal or academic writing, you would more likely use words like condescending, supercilious, disdainful, or haughty instead.
Words Close in Meaning

• Snobby / snobbish — the closest synonyms; a snob looks down on those of "lower" class or taste (snooty and snobby are nearly interchangeable in everyday use)
  • Stuck-up — informal; acting as if you're too good for others
  • Condescending — treating others as if they're less intelligent or important than you
  • Haughty — proud, cold, and disdainful
  • Arrogant — an exaggerated belief in one's own importance (broader than snooty; doesn't always involve class)
  • Supercilious — formal; showing contemptuous superiority
Opposite Words

• Down-to-earth — unpretentious, friendly regardless of status
  • Humble — modest, doesn't think of oneself as superior
  • Approachable — easy and comfortable to talk to
  • Unpretentious — not trying to appear more important or refined than one is
A Quick Mental Image to Remember It

Imagine a person at a party who greets a well-dressed guest with a warm smile, then turns to look at a casually dressed stranger with a cool, barely-there nod before slowly turning away. They didn't say anything openly rude — but the message was clear: "You're not on my level."

That person is snooty.
